article.Citation/Title: Jovaisa T, Laurinenas, G., Vosylius, S., Sipylaite, J., Badaras, R., & Ivaskevicius, J. (2006). Effects of ketamine on precipitated opiate withdrawal. Medicina (Kaunas), 42(8), 625-634.
article.Outcome: OOWS-A withdrawal-severity score significantly lower (less severe withdrawal) in Ketamine vs Control group
article.InterventionDescription: Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg bolus + 0.5 mg/kg/h IV infusion vs saline placebo during general anesthesia for rapid naloxone/naltrexone opiate-antagonist induction in opiate-dependent inpatients.

ae_events.Description: Hospital admission for trauma during the 4-month follow-up period, one of four such admissions; authors state unrelated to RAI.
Hospital admission for acute pancreatitis during the 4-month follow-up period, one of four such admissions; authors state unrelated to RAI.
Hospital admission for ulcerative colitis during the 4-month follow-up period, one of four such admissions; authors state unrelated to RAI.
Patient relapsed to regular opiate use, developed injection-related sepsis, and died in hospital during the 4-month follow-up; not attributed to RAI/ketamine by authors.

article.Outcome: No explicit 'primary outcome' is labelled anywhere in the article. The study measures cardiovascular/respiratory/renal/GI response, cortisol, OOWS-A withdrawal severity (acute phase), rescue-medication use (early postanesthetic phase), and 4-month abstinence/retention. Per precedence rule (2) (no author-designated primary -> use the SUD-behavioral outcome the abstract leads with), the abstract's Results paragraph opens with 'Ketamine group presented better control of withdrawal symptoms' -- this maps to the Objective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (OOWS-A), the study's dedicated opiate-withdrawal-severity instrument, which per this prompt's boundary-case guidance is itself an SUD outcome. Body text states 'Opiate withdrawal scores on OOWS-A scale were significantly higher in Control group... (Fig. 2 and 3)' and the Fig. 2 caption gives 'difference between groups significant for hourly OOWS-A score, p<0.05.' No group means/SDs for OOWS-A are given in extractable text (only in an OCR-garbled figure image), so Outcome is coded as a directional descriptor rather than a number. Note: the most numerically detailed outcome in the article is actually cardiovascular response (Table 3: MAP/HR means, SDs, 95% CIs, exact p-values by hour) -- this was deliberately NOT chosen as Outcome because it is not the SUD-behavioral outcome the abstract leads with, per the stated precedence order.
article.SD: No dispersion statistic for OOWS-A is given in extractable text; the underlying data exist only inside an OCR-garbled figure image (Fig. 2), which cannot be read reliably. Coded '.'.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: OOWS-A/anesthesia-phase data are reported for the same n=50 cohort used in Table 3 (Ketamine n=22, Control n=28; 22+28=50), i.e. the 'complete profiles' cohort after 8 of the original 58 enrolled/randomized patients were excluded for protocol non-compliance/incomplete data.
article.Retention (%): Denominator = 58 (all patients enrolled were also randomized on the procedure day; no separate lower randomized N is reported). The study's own three-phase design (anesthetic, 48-hour postanesthetic, 4-month remote) makes the 4-month remote phase part of 'the study,' so completers = 45 (patients with 4-month outcome data). 45/58 = 77.6%, which is within 2 points of the 80% threshold that flips a downstream methodological-quality cell -- flagged per instructions. Note the alternate figure: 50/58 = 86.2% completed only the in-hospital (acute + 48-hour) phases before the 8 protocol-noncompliance exclusions; 77.6% was used because it reflects completion of the full study through its longest planned follow-up.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: No a priori or post hoc power/sample-size justification is given anywhere (sample_size_power=N), and the Acknowledgements only thank the Lithuanian AIDS Center for laboratory support -- there is no funding-source statement or conflict-of-interest disclosure for the study itself (funding_coi=N). All other 12 criteria are explicitly described (including harms, via 'There were no complications related to anesthesia phase or opiate antagonist induction' and the remote-phase complications/hospitalizations/death account). 12/14 met, below the 13-of-14 threshold, so MethodologyDescribedYN=0.

article.BaseStatus: No explicit baseline-severity label or standardized severity score is reported. Inferred 'Severe' from: enrollment required a formal ICD-10/DSM-IV diagnosis of opiate 'dependence' (the more severe diagnostic category, vs. 'abuse'/harmful use), a required dependence duration >1 year, and a mean morphine stabilization dose of ~55-58 mg/day prior to RAI. This is an inference, not an author-stated severity rating.
article.Country_USvsNonUS: Study conducted at Vilnius University Emergency Hospital, Vilnius, Lithuania. Coded 'NonUS'; actual country recorded here per instructions.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: Race/ethnicity is never reported anywhere in the article (Lithuanian cohort). Coded '.'.
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: Sample was restricted to age 18-35 and ASA physical-status I-II (no/minor comorbidities), and explicitly excluded polysubstance abuse, current long-acting-opioid use, and acute medical/surgical conditions -- narrower than a typical real-world treatment-seeking opiate-dependent population, which commonly includes polysubstance use and comorbidity. Coded 0 (not representative).
article.InterventionTherapy: Patients were required to have an aftercare plan (outpatient counseling or residential rehabilitation) before RAI and were later tracked for retention in it, but this aftercare was a post-discharge program the patient chose independently, not a therapy/counseling/integration component delivered as part of the drug-administration protocol itself (which occurred entirely under general anesthesia). Coded 0.
article.MediatingYN: Cortisol (a candidate neuroendocrine intermediate) was measured and its trajectory discussed as a possible mechanism ('this pattern may be caused by non-NMDA-mediated activation of hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis'), but no formal mediation/indirect-effect model was fit — narrative mechanistic speculation only, so 0 rather than 1 or 3.
article.ModeratingYN: Baseline characteristics (age, sex, morphine stabilization dose, prior detoxifications) were measured and compared for balance (Table 2) but never tested as effect modifiers via an interaction term or stratified analysis, so 0 rather than 1 or 3.
article.HypothesisTestReportedYN: OOWS-A group differences are reported as statistically significant (p<0.05) each hour of the anesthesia phase (Fig. 2), satisfying the 'any inferential signal for the primary outcome' bar even though the exact statistic is not printed.
article.MentalHealthChangeMeasured: The 4-month follow-up questionnaire (based on the Addiction Severity Index) explicitly screened for 'new onset of psychopathology or compulsive behavior,' which is coded as measurement of a mental-health outcome, even though no named psychometric depression/anxiety scale was used.
article.QualityOfLifeMeasured: The 4-month ASI-based questionnaire covered health status, social/family life, and legal status, but no dedicated quality-of-life instrument (e.g., SF-36, WHOQOL) is named or used. Coded 0.
article.Followup in months: Longest reported follow-up is 4 months post-procedure (the study's third, 'remote' phase, per its own stated three-phase design: anesthetic, 48-hour postanesthetic, and 4-month remote). Measured from end of the RAI/anesthesia treatment episode, consistent with the article's own phase framework; only one follow-up horizon (4 months) is reported for remote outcomes, so there is no baseline-vs-end-of-treatment discrepancy to reconcile.
article.MortalityMeasured: Coded 1 because a death (injection-related sepsis after relapse to opiate use) is reported among the 4-month outcome data, not because the study used a dedicated mortality endpoint/instrument. Per instructions, a death reported only as an adverse event still sets this field to 1 and generates an ae_events row (Jovaisa T 2006_AE04).
article.Pos Result Y/N: Coded 1 based on the primary withdrawal-severity outcome (OOWS-A) and related acute/early-postanesthetic measures (rescue clonazepam/carbamazepine doses, morning cortisol) all favoring Ketamine with p<0.05 or p<0.001. Note: the 4-month outcomes (abstinence, retention, opiate-free weeks) showed no significant between-group difference ('Differences between groups are statistically insignificant'), so positivity is confined to the acute/short-term withdrawal-suppression endpoints, not sustained long-term recovery outcomes -- consistent with the article's own conclusion.
article.Funding/COI YN: No funding-source statement or conflict-of-interest disclosure is given for the study. The Acknowledgements section only thanks the Lithuanian AIDS Center for performing laboratory analysis, which is an in-kind lab-support acknowledgement, not a funding/COI statement. Coded 0.
article.EligibleYN: Criterion (a): met -- prospectively planned RCT (randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind), defined enrollment (n=58), an assigned regimen (ketamine vs. saline infusion), and prospective outcome assessment across three planned phases. Criterion (b): met -- OOWS-A/SOWS opiate-withdrawal-severity scores are a withdrawal outcome, which this prompt's boundary-case guidance explicitly treats as an SUD outcome; the 4-month follow-up additionally reports abstinence, opiate-free weeks, and relapse to opiate use. Both criteria satisfied -> EligibleYN=Y.

ae_events.Jovaisa T 2006_AE01: Article states '4 patients admitted to hospital in a 4-month period for trauma, acute pancreatitis, and ulcerative colitis' without a per-condition participant breakdown, so NAffected is coded '.' for this and the two related entries (AE02, AE03); total across the three conditions is 4 patients. Hospitalization itself meets the FDA 'inpatient hospitalization' seriousness criterion, so graded Severe via the rubric (authors did not assign a formal CTCAE grade or SAE label -- SeveritySource=rubric). SeverityIndeterminate is coded N because the hospitalization signal alone is sufficient for a confident Severe grading regardless of the missing per-condition detail. Authors state these events are unrelated to RAI; captured here regardless of attribution per the instruction that understating harm is the cardinal AE error. Group (Ketamine vs. Control) is not specified for these patients, so the article-level ArmScope is coded 'pooled'.
ae_events.Jovaisa T 2006_AE02: See Jovaisa T 2006_AE01 -- same source sentence and same reasoning (hospitalization -> Severe via FDA seriousness criterion; NAffected unknown per-condition; arm not specified).
ae_events.Jovaisa T 2006_AE03: See Jovaisa T 2006_AE01 -- same source sentence and same reasoning (hospitalization -> Severe via FDA seriousness criterion; NAffected unknown per-condition; arm not specified).
ae_events.Jovaisa T 2006_AE04: Text: 'One more patient returned to regular opiate use, developed injection-related sepsis, and later died in hospital' -- 'one more' confirms this patient is distinct from the four hospitalized above, giving NParticipantsWithAE=5 total. Death is CTCAE Grade 5 / meets the FDA 'death' seriousness criterion by definition, graded Severe via rubric (authors did not assign a formal grade; SeveritySource=rubric). Authors frame this as a consequence of relapse rather than of RAI/ketamine; captured regardless of attribution. Arm not specified in the text.

config_proposal.metric: Objective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (OOWS-A) group difference (narrative only)
config_proposal.note: OOWS-A group difference (Ketamine < Control, i.e., less severe withdrawal) is reported only as significant per-hour (p<0.05) in the Fig. 2 caption and body text; no group means, SDs, or a test statistic with degrees of freedom are given in extractable text -- the underlying values exist only inside an OCR-garbled figure image -- so no defensible conversion to a standardized effect size (d/g/eta_p/F/chi2/OR/RR) is possible.
config_proposal.tier2_basis: Direction and statistical significance (favors ketamine, p<0.05) are established for the primary withdrawal-severity outcome (OOWS-A), and related acute-phase measures (rescue medication doses, cortisol) corroborate the direction, but no means/SD or computable effect size are available in extractable text to judge magnitude, precluding small/moderate/large classification. The 4-month (long-term) outcomes showed no significant between-group difference.
